framing_assertion.rationale: The initial request ('chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds') asserts that the backlog is caused by slow responses to questions, framed by SH-SUP who has a stated bias toward response-speed framing.

hypotheses.statement: Customers wait because support agents are slow to respond to refund-status questions in tickets; a chatbot answering questions faster would resolve the backlog.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's own framing and the stated justification for the chatbot solution; SH-SUP's noted bias ('frames everything as response speed') means this needs independent verification before being adopted.

hypotheses.statement: The underlying refund payment processing itself is slow, so customers keep messaging for updates regardless of how fast agents reply; a chatbot would not fix the root delay.
hypotheses.rationale: If the real bottleneck is backend payment processing (DA-PAY) rather than communication, a chatbot addresses symptoms only and the real fix is a process/system change in P-REF.

hypotheses.statement: Customers lack self-service visibility into refund status, so they open tickets just to ask 'where is my refund', even if agent response times are reasonable.

hypotheses.statement: The backlog stems from high ticket volume relative to support staffing/capacity, not from any particular slowness in answering or processing refunds.

key_points: The support lead (SH-SUP) initially framed the backlog as caused by slow agent responses (CL-01, CL-02, E-03), proposing a chatbot as the fix.

Investigation found payment-db shows 5 refunds R-0..R-4 outright failed with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01/F-01), and ticket-db shows a 2.0h median first-response time against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02/F-02) — agents are fast, not slow.

These findings contradict the chatbot framing: hypothesis H-SLOW-RESPONSE is REJECTED (contradicted by E-01, E-02), while H-REFUND-IBAN-FAILURE is SUPPORTED (E-01) as the confirmed mechanism, per conflicts C-1 through C-7 on the same assertion.
The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring the critical unknown of what share of the 900-ticket backlog is actually caused by the 5 IBAN failures to VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION.

The release scope is limited to compiling/analyzing the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund records from payment-db (work item W-WI-1-IBAN-FAILURE-RECORDS, DONE); correlating tickets to refunds (DA-TCK) was intentionally excluded from this release.
Decision: RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds — the confirmed root-cause finding (5 failed refunds) is released, but attribution/correlation work and any fix are not.

A required-before-production verification obligation (VOB-R-2) remains open: whether FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT is confined to these 5 historical records or is an ongoing systemic payment-db validation defect (U-IBAN-DEFECT-SCOPE), unresolved because DA-PAY completeness is marked UNKNOWN.
limitations_explained: Backlog attribution is unquantified: only 5 failed refunds and a 900-ticket population are established, with no confirmed linkage between them, so the correlation/attribution analysis is withheld pending VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION (status OPEN, impact HIGH).
No write access exists to correct the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds or to fix the intake validation defect, so this release cannot remove the root cause itself — it only documents the finding.

Whether this is a one-time historical issue (5 records) or an ongoing systemic defect that will keep generating new IBAN failures is unresolved (U-IBAN-DEFECT-SCOPE, VOB-R-2 open, required BEFORE_PRODUCTION) because payment-db (DA-PAY) completeness is marked UNKNOWN.

The assumption that the 900-ticket sample (ticket-db) is representative for assessing causality, and that ticket-db's schema even supports direct refund-ID linkage, is itself unconfirmed (A-TICKET-POPULATION-REPRESENTA), limiting confidence in any future correlation result.

Strengthening IBAN-format validation at refund-submission intake, which would prevent recurrence, was identified as a remedy (SR-R3-INTAKE-VALIDATION-FIX) but marked not feasible within the available time and left unfinished.
output.summary: The stakeholder (SH-SUP) requested a chatbot, framing the refund ticket backlog as caused by slow agent response (CL-01, CL-02, E-03). Analysis instead found that 5 refunds (R-0..R-4) in payment-db fail outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), while ticket-db shows a 2.0h median response time against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02) — ruling out slow response as the cause (hypothesis H-SLOW-RESPONSE REJECTED) and supporting a payment-processing defect instead (H-REFUND-IBAN-FAILURE SUPPORTED). This is the root problem as defined in PD-1. The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring the open question of how much of the 900-ticket backlog is actually attributable to these 5 failures (VOB-U-BACKLOG-ATTRIBUTION). The release delivers only the confirmed, scoped finding — the compiled list of 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund records from payment-db — and withholds the ticket-to-refund correlation work and any fix. The decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION (no holds): what is released is verified and evidence-backed, but attribution, systemic-defect scope, and remediation are explicitly out of scope and flagged as known limitations rather than silently resolved.
